members.tone: The plain word for it, and still an accusation - it names a settled disposition to cheat, not one bad day.
Judges the breach of a code rather than the lie itself; what is lost is standing, not just truth.
A near-archaic use, and the pun softens it - the double-dealing sounds almost like a skill.
Puts the intent in view: not merely wrong, but meaning to mislead.
Names the betrayal of someone who trusted you - the harm is to a relationship, not to the truth.
The coldest word in the family; it implies a practised double life rather than a single deception.
Blunt and personal - the accusation you make to someone's face, or behind their back.
The flatter, less quotable cousin of two-faced; the same charge with none of the sting.
Biblical in flavour - it condemns the mouth rather than the man.
The one near-flattering word here: the deception is pleasant enough that being taken in sounds enjoyable.
Aims at the reasoning, not the character - an argument can be fallacious with nobody lying.
The legal word: it implies a crime has been committed, not merely a lie told.
Mild because it does not require a liar - a shadow or a photograph can be deceptive.
Stops short of accusation: it reports the effect, and leaves the intent unstated.
Said of things rather than people - a false name, a false wall; the object was built to deceive.
Not a judgement but a literary label, for the rogue-hero tradition where the trickery is the entertainment.
Warm without being showy: it says a thing is what it claims, and that this was worth saying.
Borrowed from German by critics; it praises the real thing while advertising the speaker's taste.
Carries the weight of proof - used where provenance has actually been checked.
Legal in origin: it certifies good faith rather than admiring it.
Praises by refusing to entertain doubt - it closes the argument rather than winning it.
Almost always emphasis rather than proof; a veritable feast is not being authenticated.
Procedural warmth only: someone has testified, and that is all it claims.
The bureaucratic word - a certificate exists somewhere, and the object is the better for it.
Praises the paperwork and says nothing about worth.
The plainest way to say a note or a passport is not forged; no compliment is intended.
Of a thing rather than a person - honest money, honest weight; it lends objects a moral character.
Emphatic and colloquial: it swears to the thing instead of proving it.
The polite version, with the oath taken out.
Homely and regional; the emphasis of someone who expects to be doubted.
The unarguable positive: it describes behaviour nobody objects to and implies nothing further.
Praises ease of manner in someone who need not have bothered - it fits people with standing.
Mild, slightly old-fashioned praise; pleasantness rather than depth.
Warm in form rather than in feeling - a cordial greeting can be perfectly correct and quite cold.
Warmth that puts a room at ease; usually said of hosts.
Faintly disapproving of other people's friendships - it hints the closeness came too fast or too conveniently.
British and blokeish: friendly in a way that insists on being equals.
Usually raises an eyebrow at a friendship that looks more like an arrangement.
Openly mocking - the reduplication does the sneering for you.
Technical and cool; used of marriages and arrangements rather than of feelings.
Carries political history: warmth between equals in a shared cause, and a faint whiff of the cause itself.
Archaic on its own; nearly always heard in the longer form.
Backhanded: it describes someone friendly to everyone, and therefore to no one in particular.
Scots for a cosy, unforced warmth; affectionate and close to untranslatable.
The commoner spelling of couthie, with the same Scots warmth.
Of an atmosphere rather than a person - and it turns critical the moment it takes an object: cozy with the regulators.
